opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd answer in two parts, because people often mean different things by "beyond the Transformer."

The first meaning is architectural: what replaces attention? There's a lot of work there: state space models, linear attention, hybrids. Those matter, but I don't think the next major advance is mainly about swapping one block for another. The Transformer won less because attention is magical and more because it scales well on hardware and is general enough not to get in the way. A new architecture that is just ten percent more efficient will help, but it won't change how we think.

The second meaning is the one I care about more: what is the next shift in how we build and understand these systems? My background is physics, and from that angle what's missing is structure and understanding. Today we mostly treat models as black boxes. We scale data and compute, watch the loss go down, and then spend a lot of effort afterward reverse-engineering what the model learned. It works, but it's expensive, and it's a bit like doing astronomy before Newton. We have amazing observations and very little theory.

So I think the next big advances will come from a few directions.

One is interpretability built into the design rather than added afterward. That was part of the motivation behind Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. Could we put the learnable nonlinearity on the edges, so that what the network learns can sometimes be read off as a formula? KANs aren't going to replace Transformers tomorrow, and I'd be the first to say they have limitations. But the broader idea, that architecture can be chosen to make learned structure visible, is something I'm confident about.

Another is a science of training dynamics. Phenomena like grokking, phase transitions in learning, and how representations form look very much like physics problems to me. There are order parameters, critical points, and emergent behavior. If we understood these the way we understand phase transitions in matter, we could train far more efficiently instead of relying on trial and error at enormous scale.

The third is AI for science, and science for AI, as a loop. Models that can discover compact, symmetric, physically meaningful structure, not just predict the next token, would be a qualitatively different kind of tool. And what we learn by asking models to do science may feed back into better architectures.

So my short answer: I don't expect a single "Transformer killer." I expect the field to move from a purely engineering, scaling-driven paradigm toward one where theory, structure, and understanding play a much bigger role. Something like the transition from alchemy to chemistry. That's the advance I'm most excited about, and honestly the one I think is most underinvested right now.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I'll be honest that I don't think the next big thing will come from stacking more clever modules on top of the Transformer. The Transformer is a remarkably general architecture, and most attempts to beat it on its own terms end up being incremental.

So I tend to come at this from a different angle, which is: what do we actually not understand about these systems? I'm a physicist by training, and in physics, when you have a phenomenon you can't explain, you don't just build a bigger version of it. You try to find the simple structure underneath. That's really what drove the work on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. We asked whether, instead of fixed activation functions on nodes with learned linear weights, you could put learnable functions on the edges. That turns out to make the network much more interpretable, because you can literally look at each edge and see the function it has learned. For scientific problems, where you want to recover a formula and not just a prediction, that matters a lot.

But I want to be careful not to oversell it. KANs are not going to replace Transformers in language modeling next year. What I think they point toward is a broader direction: architectures designed with interpretability and physical priors built in, rather than bolted on afterward. Right now we train enormous models and then spend enormous effort trying to reverse-engineer what they're doing. That feels backwards.

The other piece is what I'd call a science of deep learning. We still lack basic principles for why grokking happens, why certain representations emerge, how scaling laws arise. If we had that theory, the next architecture wouldn't be a guess. It would be derived, the way you derive a design from first principles in engineering. So if you ask me where the next major advance comes from, I'd say from understanding first, and then building. The field has mostly done it in the opposite order, and it has worked surprisingly well, but I don't think it's sustainable, especially if we want AI that scientists can actually trust and learn from.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what limitation are we trying to overcome? A new architecture is interesting, but replacing the Transformer is not necessarily the same thing as making a major advance in intelligence.

One direction I find compelling is learning useful structure from data. A model can be very good at predicting observations without giving us a simple explanation of what generates them. In science, we want to go further: identify the relevant variables, discover relationships between them, and understand when those relationships hold.

So I would look for systems that can move between flexible learning and compact, explicit representations. You might start with a neural network because you don’t know the structure of the problem. Then, as it learns, you try to extract something simpler that you can inspect and test. That understanding could also guide what data you collect next.

Whether that requires replacing the Transformer, or adding something around it, I think is still open. But the exciting advance would be a system that helps us discover explanations, not just produce increasingly accurate predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should separate two questions: what comes after the Transformer as an architecture, and what comes after the current way of doing AI. Those might have very different answers.

Architecturally, you can imagine better ways to handle memory, recurrence, or long sequences. But a new architecture by itself doesn’t necessarily give us a new kind of intelligence. The bigger question is whether we can build systems that learn from experience, discover useful abstractions, and revise their understanding of the world.

Think about how a scientist works. You don’t just absorb more text. You propose a hypothesis, design an experiment, observe what happens, and change your model. I find that loop very interesting for AI. Can a system choose which information it needs, instead of only learning from information we have already collected?

So I wouldn’t confidently predict one architecture that replaces the Transformer. The next major advance could come from changing how we train and interact with these systems, with architecture evolving to support that. For me, the exciting direction is AI that participates in discovering knowledge.
